input:
Scope

This review is concerned with the rapidly developing field of membrane separations for solvent recovery, an area in which a membrane is used to separate a solvent from a dissolved solute, from a second solvent, or from a more complex mixture, so that the solvent in question can be returned to the process that produced the stream in the first place. In total, the review covers 45 papers that have been published over the course of the last 12 years. Work is included where the membrane operates on a liquid process stream and where the objective is the recovery of the solvent for the purposes of reuse. By contrast, work on desalination and on gas separation falls outside the boundary of the review, as does work in which the solvent is recovered only as a product of a reaction work-up rather than from a stream that the process generates on a continuous basis. The literature can be divided according to membrane material and according to the separation that is demanded of the membrane, and the review follows this division throughout: polymeric membranes and ceramic membranes are treated as separate bodies of work, reflecting the fact that their behaviour in organic solvents differs in kind and not merely in degree. It should also be noted that terminology is not uniform across the field, and the review accordingly uses the terms of each individual paper where a result is reported, before any comparison is drawn between results.

Established results

It is now well established that the separation of solvents from dissolved solutes by means of membranes can be achieved at laboratory scale across a wide range of solvent and solute pairs. Membranes that are capable of retaining the solute while at the same time passing the solvent have been reported for feeds that would damage a large proportion of the polymeric materials that are in common use, and the work that has been carried out on ceramic membranes demonstrates that solvent resistance, which represented the first major obstacle in the field, can be overcome, in the sense that there are materials on both sides of the material division that are able to withstand the solvents in question. Performance is defined by flux and rejection taken together, and the pattern that emerges from the reported results is essentially a trade-off between the two: a membrane that is tightened in order to raise its rejection will pass solvent more slowly, and the reported results arrange themselves along this trade-off rather than above it. Solvent stability, it is important to appreciate, is reported as a test outcome rather than as a service record; membranes that are described as stable have been exposed to the solvent under test conditions for the duration of a trial, and what the result establishes is behaviour over that period of exposure. Finally, the concentration of a solute by the removal of solvent is established as a unit operation at laboratory scale, with the membrane step placed either ahead of, or in place of, a thermal separation, and the energy comparison that motivates the field as a whole rests on the avoidance of the phase change that a thermal step would require.

Disagreements

It is in the area of the rejection of dissolved solutes that the literature is most clearly in disagreement with itself, and this disagreement represents the largest open question to emerge from the material reviewed here. The same class of membrane is reported in one body of work as retaining a solute almost completely, and in another body of work as passing a substantial proportion of it, under conditions that the papers themselves describe in broadly similar terms. Unfortunately, the disagreement does not resolve on a closer inspection of the reported conditions, because the conditions that actually decide rejection are not the conditions that the papers report most carefully: the feed composition at the membrane surface, the state of the membrane following its exposure to the solvent, and the duration over which the rejection was measured all differ from one report to another, and each of these factors is capable, on its own, of moving the figure that is obtained. Conditioning, in particular, is reported in a highly uneven fashion. A membrane that is measured after prolonged contact with the solvent is not in the same state as a membrane that is measured on first contact, and those papers that do not state the conditioning that was applied leave their rejection figures effectively unanchored. The conflict should therefore be understood as a conflict of method rather than as a conflict of material: until such time as rejection is reported against a stated conditioning and a stated measurement duration, the literature will continue to contain two different values for one and the same quantity, with no agreed means of choosing between them.

Gaps

Perhaps the most striking gap in the literature is the measurement that nobody appears to report, namely the performance of a membrane over extended continuous operation. Papers routinely report the flux and the rejection of a membrane at the start of a trial, and some go on to report the same pair of quantities again at the end of a trial, but the course of performance between those two points, and indeed beyond the longest trial that has been reported, is essentially absent from the literature that has been reviewed. This is a significant omission, because a recovery unit in an actual process runs continuously, and its membrane is purchased on the expectation that its performance will persist over time; the literature offers the initial value and, at best, a final value, and nothing whatsoever on the trajectory that connects the two, or on the point at which replacement of the membrane becomes necessary. A second gap follows directly from the first: because extended operation remains unmeasured, the effect of cleaning on a membrane that has been run in solvent service is likewise unreported, and no paper in the set establishes whether performance that has been lost in operation can be recovered by cleaning or whether that loss is, in fact, permanent. In summary, the field is in a position to state what its membranes do when they are new; it is not yet in a position to state what they do in service, and it is precisely that measurement that the next body of work will need to supply if the field is to move forward.

Established results

Separation of solvents from dissolved solutes by membranes is established at laboratory scale across a wide range of solvent and solute pairs. Membranes that retain the solute while passing the solvent are reported for feeds that would damage a large part of the polymeric materials in common use, and the ceramic work establishes that solvent resistance, which was the first obstacle in the field, has materials on both sides of the material division that withstand the solvents in question. Solvent stability is reported as a test outcome and not as a service record; membranes described as stable have been exposed to the solvent under test conditions for the duration of a trial, and the result establishes behaviour over that exposure. The trade between flux and rejection is reported as a property of each membrane rather than of the operating point, and the review treats it on those terms. A result that appears to escape the trade does so, on inspection, by reporting the two quantities under different conditions, and such results are recorded here as reports under differing conditions and not as exceptions. Stability claims carry the same discipline: a membrane stable in a solvent over a trial has been shown stable over that trial, and the established result is the trial result, with its duration as part of the claim.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the rejection of dissolved solutes, and the conflict is the largest open disagreement in the literature reviewed. The same class of membrane is reported in one body of work as retaining a solute almost completely and in another as passing a substantial part of it, under conditions the papers describe in similar terms. The disagreement does not resolve on inspection of the reported conditions, because the conditions that decide rejection are not the conditions the papers report most carefully: feed composition at the membrane surface, the state of the membrane after exposure to the solvent, and the duration over which rejection was measured all differ between reports, and each is capable of moving the figure. Conditioning is reported unevenly. A membrane measured after prolonged contact with the solvent is not in the state of a membrane measured on first contact, and papers that do not state the conditioning leave their rejection figures unanchored. The conflict therefore stands as a conflict of method rather than of material: until rejection is reported against a stated conditioning and a stated measurement duration, the literature contains two values for the same quantity and no agreed means of choosing between them.

A resolution of the conflict is available in principle and absent in practice. Rejection reported against a stated feed composition at the membrane surface, a stated conditioning, and a stated measurement duration would make the two bodies of work commensurable, and the disagreement would then be a measurement the field could repeat. No convention of that kind is in use across the papers reviewed, and the review does not impose one retrospectively, because the conditioning and the duration cannot be recovered from papers that did not record them.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is performance over extended continuous operation. Papers report the flux and the rejection of a membrane at the start of a trial, and some report the pair again at the end of a trial, but the course of performance between those points, and beyond the longest trial, is absent from the literature reviewed. A recovery unit in a process runs continuously, and its membrane is bought on the expectation that performance persists; the literature offers the initial value and, at best, a final value, and nothing on the trajectory that connects them or on the point at which replacement becomes necessary. A second gap follows from the first: because extended operation is unmeasured, the effect of cleaning on a membrane that has run in solvent service is also unreported, and no paper in the set establishes whether performance lost in operation is recovered by cleaning or is permanent. The field can state what its membranes do when new. It cannot yet state what they do in service, and that is the measurement the next body of work has to supply.

The gap also limits what the established results can be used for. A design taken from the literature carries an initial flux and an initial rejection into a duty that runs for years, and every quantity derived from those values inherits the absence. Until extended operation is measured and reported as a course of values rather than as endpoints, solvent recovery by membrane remains established as a separation and unestablished as a service, and the distinction belongs in any use made of the results reviewed here.
